newsitem.title: JAPAN: Another Japan firm to offer cheap Internet access.
newsitem.headline: Another Japan firm to offer cheap Internet access.

text.p: Japan Telecom Co Ltd, one of the nation's three long-distance carriers, announced plans on Thursday to offer a new Internet service that could mean hotter competition and lower costs for journeys in cyberspace.

The company said it would launch a computer network service next April that would provide individual users with inexpensive dial-up to the Internet, in direct competition with another service by Japanese telephone giant NTT.
The move shows that competition in the computer communications market is heating up in Japan, where the Internet got off to a relatively slow start but is now seeing explosive growth in demand.

A Japan Telecom spokesman said the Open Data Network (ODN) will be cheaper to use than Nippon Telegraph and Telephone Corp's (NTT) version, due to be launched in December, but did not provide actual prices.
For volume users, the company will lay low-cost dedicated cables, which can be used for such things as computer data transmission and the construction of local call networks.
NTT, a telecoms goliath, is trying to develop into new areas as deregulation threatens its commanding position in the domestic phone market.

It has said it plans to charge individual users 2,300 yen ($20) a month to access the Internet for up to 15 hours a month, which is less than the cost of most other Internet access service providers in Japan.
NTT has said that its new network service would help close the price gap between Japan and other countries for Internet use, which has come under criticism from Web surfers.
High telephone charges have so far hampered the spread of the Internet and computer communications in Japan, analysts say.
There were 270,000 Japanese host computers connected to the Internet at the end of January 1996, just 2.8 percent of the total connected on the global market.

But industry analysts expect Japan's Internet access service market will balloon to between 200 billion yen ($1.76 billion) and 300 billion yen ($2.65 billion) in 2000, up from the 25 billion yen ($221 million) in 1995.
The new networks will pose a threat to existing Internet and leased-line providers that use relatively expensive systems such as telephone exchanges.
